Digoxin is a positive inotrope used in heart failure. It works by blocking the Na+/K+ ATPase in the cardiomyocyte which causes a decrease in sodium movement into the cell. This in turn causes more sodium to be exchanged for calcium ions, causing an increase in intracellular calcium. This means that the heart can contract more strongly.

Agranulocytosis is a severe form of neutropenia characterised by a marked reduction in the absolute neutrophil count. It is an undesirable side effect of certain drugs, most commonly clozapine. Clozapine should not be used in patients with a history of agranulocytosis or neutropenia. Patients on clozapine should be monitored for signs of agranulocytosis, particularly during the initial 1-2 months of treatment. Clozapine should not be stopped, although a dose reduction may be considered if agranulocytosis is suspected. If the neutropenia is mild, a dose reduction may be sufficient to prevent the development of agranulocytosis. If the neutropenia is severe, clozapine should be stopped and an alternative antipsychotic prescribed. A dose of clozapine may be restarted after 6-8 weeks when neutrophil counts have recovered. Sentinel cells (also known as the first responder cells) are a type of phagocyte that reside in peripheral tissues, and are responsible for the detection of invading microbes and subsequent initiation of the inflammatory response. They can be activated by pathogen derived products (such as LPS) or by pattern recognition receptors (such as TLRs) on other cells. They then migrate to the site of infection, where they engulf the microbes and present their antigens on their MHC I and II molecules to T cells. Other antigen presenting cells (APCs) include macrophages and B cells.

Agranulocytosis is a severe form of neutropenia characterised by the complete absence of granulocytes on blood count. It is a serious adverse drug reaction that can be caused by some drugs of antipsychotic and anticonvulsant classes. Clozapine is the only antipsychotic which is commonly associated with agranulocytosis (along with some other rare anticonvulsants).
